structured_output.summary: I searched for outside evidence on the open time levers (H2.15, H2.16.3, H2.13.2) and the open accuracy levers (H6.5.3, H6.7), and looked for directions the tree has not considered. No public CIFAR-100 leaderboard beats the tree's results: the AIDDA repo has no PRs, and the only public CIFAR-100 recipe is futurebiohackers, at 8.11 s on Modal. The useful findings fall into three groups. (1) H2.15 is backed by primary sources. airbench says it disables the whitening-bias gradient "to increase backward-pass throughput … without reducing accuracy". hiverge does the freeze by detaching the bias in forward (b.detach()), so the stem output needs no grad and autograd skips group-1 conv1's dgrad, the stem GELU backward and the bias reduction. My FLOP count puts the dgrad alone at ~1.9% of conv FLOPs per step, so the saving could exceed the 0.5-1.5% estimate. Fable's e1, by contrast, only zeroes the LR, which saves nothing, like E061. (2) H2.16.3 looks infeasible from first principles. BN backward needs per-channel reductions over all of N·H·W before dX can be written. One 32 px activation (~378 MB) is far larger than the A100's on-chip memory. PyTorch's fused normalization backward (MixOrderReduction, torch 2.11) only works when a row fits on-chip (≤16384 elements) and targets LayerNorm/RMSNorm. The two-pass structure that E067 profiled is therefore already the minimum without cuDNN conv-epilogue fusion (genStats), which torch 2.4 does not expose. (3) NVIDIA's tile-quantization guidance (multiples of 64, ideally 256) explains E050: 352 channels round up to 384 on 128-wide tiles. 320 likely does too, so 256 is the clean width point to test. New directions: hiverge and Fable linearly decay the Muon renorm target magnitude from 0.50 to 0.079, a zero-cost knob absent from the tree. Fable's e1 uses LS 0.09, BN eps 1e-12 with frozen BN weights, and brightness/contrast jitter. For H6.7, the label-smoothing schedule literature conflicts: TSLA says to drop LS late, which is the opposite direction to H6.7. EfficientNetV2's +0.7-0.8 pp did not include LS. So H6.7's prior should drop.

findings.claim: airbench: 'The biases are trained for 3 epochs, after which we disable their gradient to increase backward-pass throughput, which improves training speed without reducing accuracy.' BatchNorm affine scale is disabled (bias-only BN).
findings.relevance: Primary-source support that a real requires_grad freeze of the whitening bias is a backward-throughput (time) lever, not just a regularizer. E061 (LR=0) only showed the accuracy side.

findings.claim: hiverge freezes the whitening bias by detaching it in forward: x = F.conv2d(x, self.whiten.weight, b if whiten_bias_grad else b.detach()), with whiten.weight.requires_grad=False and whiten_bias_grad = step < whiten_bias_train_steps passed into a compiled forward_step.
findings.relevance: Shows the exact mechanism. Once both stem tensors are non-grad, the stem output carries no grad, so autograd skips the group-1 conv1 input-gradient (dgrad), the stem GELU backward and the bias-grad reduction. This is the implementation pattern H2.15.1 needs: two compiled graphs keyed on a bool, and only the 16 px phase needs both variants.

findings.claim: Fable e1 trains the whitening bias for ~0.2 epoch. After that its 'learning rate is set to zero in the graph, making parameter updates inert while maintaining exact numerical equivalence'. It does not switch requires_grad off, because the whole run is captured in one CUDA graph.
findings.relevance: Corrects H2.15's attribution. Fable does NOT skip the dgrad; it is equivalent to E061. Only airbench and hiverge (detach / requires_grad off) remove compute. H2.15's source should cite hiverge or airbench, not Fable.

findings.claim: Own FLOP estimate from airbench96-style shapes at 32 px (stem 24 ch at 31x31; groups 128/384/576, 3 convs each, pooling after conv1). Group-1 conv1 forward is ~26.6M MAC/img and the whole net forward is ~474M MAC/img, so fwd+bwd is ~1.42G MAC/img. Skipping only g1-conv1's dgrad removes ~1.9% of conv FLOPs per step at every resolution. That dgrad has 24 output channels, so its tensor-core efficiency is poor and its time share likely exceeds its FLOP share. Skipping the stem GELU backward and the bias reduction over 1536x24x31x31 removes extra memory traffic on top.
findings.relevance: Puts the H2.15.1 expected saving at ~1-2.5% of time, above the hypothesis's 0.5-1.5%. It is a FLOP/byte lever, so it should transfer to the 300 W PCIe judge. Suggest raising the H2.15.1 prediction threshold to >=1%.

findings.claim: PyTorch's fused normalization backward (MixOrderReduction: dX inner reduction fused with the dW/dB outer reduction) arrived around torch 2.11. It is for LayerNorm/RMSNorm and applies only to 'reasonable shapes where … a single row can fit adequately in a thread block, generally <= 16384'. Without it, the separate dX and dW/dB kernels read dY twice.
findings.relevance: In BN backward, the per-channel reductions (sum dy, sum dy·xhat) span N·H·W, e.g. 1536·31·31 ≈ 1.48M elements per channel at 32 px. The whole activation (~378 MB fp16 for group 1) is far larger than A100's on-chip memory (40 MB L2). dX cannot be written until those global reductions finish, so a one-pass 'read dy and x once' BN backward is impossible. The 2-pass structure (reduce, then apply) is already the floor. The only further fusion is moving the stats into the conv epilogue, which torch 2.4 does not expose. H2.16.3 looks infeasible as stated; recommend retiring it.

findings.claim: cuDNN's conv-BN fusion for training uses Scale_Bias_Activation_convolution_genStats in forward and Scale_Bias_Activation_ConvBwdFilter in backward: BN statistics are produced in the conv epilogue through the cuDNN backend graph API.
findings.relevance: This is the only known way to remove a BN pass, and it needs the cuDNN graph API, which PyTorch 2.4 does not expose. Writing a custom Triton conv to replace it would be very high effort. This confirms that H2.16's last lever has a very low expected value.

findings.claim: NVIDIA guidance: conv channel counts should be divisible by 8 for FP16 tensor cores, and 'by at least 64 and ideally 256 to enable efficient tiling'. Sizes that do not divide into tiles waste work (tile quantization).
findings.relevance: Explains E050 (352 channels saved half the FLOP-proportional time). On 128-wide N-tiles, 352 rounds up to 3 tiles, the same work as 384. 320 also rounds up to 384 on 128-tiles (it is clean only on 64-tiles), so H2.13.2's prediction that 320 recovers >=80% may fail for the same reason. The clean test point is 256, or reading the chosen cuDNN kernel's tile shape from the profiler names.

findings.claim: hiverge renormalizes Muon-managed filters to a target magnitude that decays linearly: target = 0.5012*(1-progress) + 0.0786*progress. Fable e1 uses the same 0.5012->0.0786 schedule, with normalization frequency going from 2 to 17 over the run.
findings.relevance: New, untested, zero-cost direction. The tree adopted hiverge's renorm cadence (E035) but never mentions the target-norm schedule. The filters feed BN, so the weight norm sets the relative update size (Muon step / ||w||). A decaying target acts as a second, implicit LR schedule. First check whether the tip renorms to a constant norm; if it does, porting the linear target decay is a cheap accuracy candidate under the H4 rule (off-seed seeds 3-10 A/B plus scored runs).

findings.claim: Fable e1 (CIFAR-10): BN momentum 0.5566 (torch momentum ≈0.443), eps=1e-12, BN weight frozen. Loss is cross-entropy with LS 0.09 and reduction='sum'. bs 1536. OrthoMomentum (NS, 3 iterations) lr 0.2255, momentum 0.655. GPU brightness ±0.14 / contrast ±0.13 jitter. The decay ends at 8.5 epochs, then a low-LR tail runs to 8.875 epochs (~4%) with an EMA (0.7 decay every 4 steps) that removes 'the ±0.1-0.2% plateau wobble'.
findings.relevance: The Fable tail was designed to reduce end-of-run variance ('plateau wobble'), not to raise the mean. So H6.5.3's ablation might find that the final EMA mainly lowers per-seed variance. That still helps the 40-seed gate, but it should be measured as an sd reduction, not only a mean gain. Fable's LS 0.09 on CIFAR-10 is consistent with E037 being null on CIFAR-100.

findings.claim: LAWA (latest weight averaging) finds that uniform averaging of the k latest checkpoints beats EMA-style weighting. With BatchNorm, the averaged model's BN statistics are unknown, and parameters tolerate larger averaging windows than BN stats do. Recomputing BN stats for the averaged model recovers full performance.
findings.relevance: Bears on the tail ablation. The tip's final EMA uses BN buffers copied from the net, which mismatch the averaged weights. A uniform average of the last 2-3 snapshots, or a different window, is the natural tuning axis if the EMA component carries the gain. E018 showed BN re-estimation hurt, though, so do not add a BN recalibration pass.

findings.claim: TSLA (Two-Stage Label Smoothing) uses label smoothing in early epochs and drops it later. On CIFAR-100 ResNet-18 (200 epochs) the best result came from switching LS off at epoch ~160, i.e. late training benefits from less smoothing.
findings.relevance: Points the opposite way from H6.7.1, which lowers LS early and keeps 0.3 late. Separately, EfficientNetV2's +0.7-0.8 pp adaptive regularization covered dropout, RandAugment and mixup, not LS (https://arxiv.org/html/2104.00298). The direct support for a phase-dependent LS in the direction H6.7 proposes is therefore weak. Both are long-schedule results, and the loss-side line just failed twice (E037, E078). Lower H6.7's prior. If a phase-LS run is done at all, the TSLA direction (lower LS in the final ~20%) is the better-supported arm.

findings.claim: The CIFAR-100 speedrun repo (an AIDDA-Institute mirror; the AIDDA repo shows 0 PRs) has no public leaderboard. Its verified ResNet-9 baseline is 75.36% at 59.30 s. The only public competitive CIFAR-100 recipe found is futurebiohackers PR #3 (75.29%, 8.11 s on Modal A100-SXM4).
findings.relevance: No external CIFAR-100 recipe is ahead of the current tip (~4.58 s). Further gains must come from the tree's own levers or from CIFAR-10 speedrun transfers (hiverge, Fable, airbench).

findings.claim: Without its reward-hacking changes (augmentation moved outside the timed region, thermal cooldown sleeps, host selection), Fable's CIFAR-10 run improves on the 1.98 s SOTA by 7.6% (to 1.828 s). Progressive resizing is the main legitimate contributor; no per-component ablation (CUDA graph, optimizer fusion, pooling) is published.
findings.relevance: Confirms that no hidden large lever remains in Fable's legitimate changes beyond what the tree already has (resizing, max-pool fix, tail). The whole-run CUDA graph is closed here (E052: 98-100% GPU-busy).
